reading.intro: Maya flies home for two weeks. At the gate she sits next to a man with a very large suitcase, and the flight is late.
reading.photos[0].caption: Flaggen vor dem Europaparlament: Deutschland, Spanien, Griechenland …
reading.photos[1].caption: Die Grenze: ein Schild, kein Zaun. Zwischen Luxemburg und Deutschland.
reading.en: Man: Excuse me, is this flight 877 to Toronto? · Maya: Yes. But it's an hour late. · Man: An hour! Typical. Are you from Canada? · Maya: Yes, from Vancouver. But I live in Berlin. And you? · Man: I'm from Turkey, from Izmir. I've lived in Frankfurt for twenty years. I'm flying to my daughter. She lives in Toronto. · Maya: Do you speak English? · Man: A little. Turkish, German, a bit of English. My daughter speaks four languages. And you? · Maya: English, French and a bit of German. · Man: Your German is good! How do you know: an hour late? · Maya: The board. There: Toronto, 17:10, now 18:10. · Man: Ah. I don't have my glasses. Then let's have a coffee. The coffee here is from Italy. Everything here is from another country. · Maya: So are we.
reading.fact: Germany has nine neighbours, more than any other country in Europe: Denmark in the north, Poland and Czechia in the east, Austria and Switzerland in the south, France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands in the west.

grammar[0].subheading: The country, its language and its people
grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[0].title: Countries with die
grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[0].text: Most countries go straight after aus: aus Spanien. A few keep their article, and it changes: aus *der* Schweiz, aus *der* Türkei, aus *den* USA.
grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[1].title: No article after sein
grammar[0].blocks[1].blocks[1].text: Ich bin Spanierin — not “eine Spanierin”. Languages take a capital and no article: Ich spreche Spanisch. The four directions are nouns with *im*: Hamburg ist *im Norden*, München ist *im Süden*.
grammar[0].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[0].fact: *Deutsch* is the language and *deutsch* the adjective: *Ich spreche Deutsch*, but *ein deutsches Auto*. Nationalities are nouns, so no article after *sein*: *Ich bin Kanadierin.*
grammar[1].subheading: The compass, and where things lie
grammar[1].photo.caption: Die Autobahn: München im Süden, Hannover im Norden. Blau ist die Autobahn, gelb die Landstraße.
grammar[1].blocks[0].note: All four are der-nouns, always with im. Two join: im Südwesten, im Nordosten.
grammar[1].blocks[1].title: Von Deutschland aus · seen from Germany
grammar[1].blocks[2].title: liegen: where a place is
grammar[1].blocks[2].text: A city or a country *liegt* (lies): *Berlin liegt im Osten.* For a person use *sein*: *Ich bin im Norden.*
grammar[1].check.title: Mini-Check
grammar[1].fact: Blue signs are the *Autobahn*, yellow signs the ordinary road, and the number in the box is the road, not the distance. *Westkreuz F* is the Frankfurt west junction, not a town.
document.caption: Die Anzeigetafel am Flughafen Frankfurt: Wohin fliegen die Flugzeuge?
document.intro: A real departures board. Find the cities, the times and the gates. The board is in English, but the cities are the same words you say in German.
document.fact: German airports write *Gate* and *Terminal* in English, but say *Abflug* for departure and *Ankunft* for arrival. The board switches language every few seconds.

document.tasks[2].instruction: The board writes city names in English. Write the German name.
